q: You brief a crew of five at the pontoon before a night passage. Only you have used the VHF before. Who do you show how to send a DSC distress alert?
a: Every crew member — the skipper may be the casualty
o: Only the mate — one operator besides you is enough
Nobody — the skipper makes every distress call
Only those who hold a radio licence
why: The skipper can be the one overboard or injured; everyone aboard must be able to raise the alarm.

fig.title: Safety briefing
lines: Only the skipper has used the VHF

q: It is 0200, the wind is F5 and you come up to take your watch. The jackstays run from the bow to the cockpit. When do you clip on?
a: To a strong point by the hatch, before you leave the cabin
o: Once you are seated in the cockpit at the helm
Only when you need to go forward of the mast
As soon as you can reach the jackstay on deck
why: Clip on before you go out — falls happen stepping into the cockpit; then move the hook to the jackstay.

q: The day before a 50-mile passage you go through this check list. What does it tell you about the liferaft?
a: Too small for six and overdue — change it before sailing
o: Fine — a raft is rated for its crew plus two more
Fine — only the flares carry a date to watch
Overdue, but a 4-person raft can still take six
why: A raft must hold everyone aboard and be in date: serviced 2022 + 3 years = due 2025.

fig.title: Pre-passage check
lines: Service interval on the label: 3 years

q: You are dismasted at night 6 M off the coast. The lifeboat searching for you is now about a mile away. Which flare do you use?
a: A red handheld flare, held out downwind
o: A red parachute rocket, fired straight up
An orange smoke canister, thrown downwind
A white handheld flare, held up high
why: A rocket is for when nobody knows where you are; close in, a red handheld pinpoints you. Smoke is for daylight.

q: You have abandoned to the liferaft with the grab bag. What do you do with the EPIRB and the SART?
a: Keep the EPIRB on; put the SART up high on its pole
o: Keep the EPIRB on; lay the SART flat on the raft floor
Switch the EPIRB off now; switch on the SART later
Keep both off until you see a ship or an aircraft
why: The EPIRB stays on until the MRCC says otherwise; the SART answers X-band radar, so the higher it is, the further it shows.

fig.title: In the liferaft
lines: Grab bag: handheld VHF, flares, water

q: A crew member's lifejacket carries an AIS MOB beacon and he also wears a PLB. If he goes over at night, which one shows him on your own plotter?
a: The AIS beacon — AIS sets nearby show it at once
o: The PLB — the satellite sends it to your plotter
Both — each one shows on any plotter within 4 M
Neither — only the rescue centre can see them
why: An AIS MOB beacon is received by AIS sets nearby; a PLB's 406 MHz signal goes via satellite to the rescue centre.

q: You are about to cross a busy area in poor visibility with a passive octahedral radar reflector. How do you hoist it?
a: As high as you can, in the 'catch-rain' position
o: Just above the guardrail, one point straight up
On the pushpit, wherever it does not chafe
At the masthead, with one point straight up
why: Height adds radar range; in the catch-rain position (a corner cup facing up) an octahedral gives its strongest echo.

fig.title: Radar reflector
lines: Spare flag halyard to the spreader

q: At 2300, 8 M off, the wheel suddenly spins free: the steering cable has parted. What do you do?
a: Heave to or stop, then fit the emergency tiller
o: Call MAYDAY and wait by the radio for help
Motor on at full speed for the nearest port
Keep sailing and hope she holds her course
why: Slow or stop the boat first, then ship the emergency tiller on the rudder stock — it is aboard for this.

fig.title: Steering failure
lines: Emergency tiller in the aft locker

q: In tonight's MOB drill a fender with a light goes over without warning. What are the first actions?
a: Shout, throw the danbuoy, press MOB, one crew points
o: Start the engine, tack, then look for the light
Call the coastguard first, then turn back
Drop all sail, then sweep with the searchlight
why: Shout and throw flotation at once, mark the position, and keep one person pointing — a small light is soon lost.

fig.note: Night drill · a fender with a light

q: In the Solent at night a crew member falls in and you press MOB at once. When you get back to the MOB waypoint there is nothing there. Where is he likely to be?
a: About 0.5 M east (090°T) of the waypoint
o: At the waypoint — the stream carries you both
About 0.5 M west (270°T) of the waypoint
About 2.0 M east (090°T) of the waypoint
why: The waypoint is fixed to the ground; he moves with the water: 2.0 kn × 15 min = 0.5 M down-tide.

fig.note: Night · no lights seen at the waypoint

q: You are beating with a full crew when someone goes over the side. Using the quick-stop, what is your first move?
a: Tack at once, leaving the jib sheeted, to stop near him
o: Bear away onto a run and gybe after ten lengths
Reach off for ten lengths, then tack and come back
Drop the jib, then start the engine and turn
why: The quick-stop keeps you close: tack at once with the jib backed and the boat stops and lies near the casualty.

fig.note: Close-hauled, F4 — a crew has just gone over

q: You are on a beam reach and choose the reach-turn-reach method for a man overboard. On what point of sail do you make the final approach?
a: A close reach, so the sails can be let fly to stop
o: A broad reach, so the boat keeps up her speed
A run, so you come down on him from upwind
Close-hauled, so you can point straight at him
why: On a close reach you can spill the sails to stop and sheet in to go — speed stays under control to the pick-up.

q: You motor back to a man overboard, heading into the wind. He is now two boat lengths off the bow. What do you do with the engine?
a: Neutral, so the propeller is stopped as he comes by
o: Ahead slow until he is level with the cockpit
Astern hard to stop the boat right beside him
Ahead with more revs to hold the bow to the wind
why: A turning propeller is the main danger to a swimmer; be in neutral as he comes alongside.

fig.note: Under power, heading into the wind

q: Your man overboard is alongside, held by a line. How do you get him back aboard?
a: Lift him level, with two strops on a halyard and a winch
o: Guide him to the stern ladder and let him climb up
Lift him upright by one strop under his arms
Haul him over the rail by his lifejacket
why: After long immersion a vertical lift risks collapse, so lift level; an exhausted swimmer can't climb, and the stern pitches.

fig.title: Casualty alongside
lines: Freeboard 1.2 m; swim ladder at the stern

q: A crew member falls into the sea at 12°C. What is the greatest danger to him in the first minute?
a: Gasping and breathing in water from cold shock
o: Hypothermia setting in within that minute
The lifejacket slipping off as it inflates
Cramp in his legs that stops him swimming
why: Cold-water shock brings a gasp and fast breathing for about a minute; a lifejacket with a sprayhood keeps the airway clear.

q: You have recovered your man overboard and got him below. What do you do for him?
a: Dry clothes, wrap him up warmly, warm sweet drinks
o: A tot of brandy and a brisk rub of his limbs
A hot shower at once to warm him quickly
Walk him round the cockpit to warm him up
why: Warm gently: shelter, remove wet clothes, insulate; warm sweet drinks only if fully conscious. No alcohol, no rubbing.

fig.title: Casualty below
lines: Recovered after 25 min in the water

q: At 0300 your crew loses sight of the man overboard's light. When do you raise the alarm?
a: Now: a DSC distress alert, then MAYDAY on 16
o: After 30 minutes of searching on your own
Once your own search pattern is complete
At first light, when searchers can see him
why: A person in the water at night is in grave and imminent danger: alert at once so ships and SAR can join the search.

fig.title: 0300, man overboard
lines: Crew has lost sight of his light
Wind F5, seas 1.5 m, 10 M off

q: At anchor, a pan of oil catches fire on the stove. What do you do?
a: Smother the pan with the fire blanket and turn the gas off
o: Throw a jug of water on it to cool the oil
Carry the pan up and throw it over the side
Blast it with dry powder from close range
why: Starve it of air: lay the blanket over the pan, gas off, leave it covered; water makes burning oil erupt.

fig.title: Galley fire
lines: Pan of oil alight on the stove

q: Smoke pours from the engine box while you are motoring, and the panel shows this. What do you do?
a: Stop the engine and fuel, then discharge through the fire port
o: Open the engine box to find the fire, then spray it
Keep motoring for the harbour 2 M away
Pour buckets of seawater into the engine box
why: Shut off fuel and air; opening the box feeds the fire — use the fire port or the fixed system, box closed.

q: Acrid smoke is coming from behind the switch panel. What do you do first?
a: Battery switches off, then CO2 into the panel
o: Foam into the panel, then the batteries off
Pull the wires out by hand to stop the short
Water from the galley tap onto the panel
why: Kill the power at the battery isolators, then use CO2 or powder; never water or foam on live electrics.

fig.title: Smoke at the panel
lines: Acrid smoke behind the switch panel
Aboard: CO2, dry powder, foam, blanket

q: Your fire is now out of control. What do you do?
a: DSC alert and MAYDAY, launch the raft to windward on its painter
o: DSC alert and MAYDAY, launch the raft to leeward on its painter
Open up the cabin to clear the smoke, then fight on
Launch the raft to leeward and cut it free at once
why: Call while you can; launch upwind of the fire so smoke and flames blow away from the raft, and keep it on its painter.

fig.title: Fire out of control
lines: Wind S F4; 6 M off the coast

q: You go below in the morning and smell gas in the saloon. What do you do first?
a: Shut it off at the cylinder; no switches, ventilate
o: Run the electric bilge pump to clear the bilge
Start the engine so the blower clears the cabin
Switch the cabin fan on to blow the gas out
why: LPG sinks into the bilge and a spark ignites it: shut the cylinder, no electrics, open up, pump with the hand pump.

fig.title: Below at 0700
lines: Smell of gas in the saloon

q: The bilge alarm wakes you at 0400 and you find this. What do you do first?
a: Pump and find the source — taste, seacocks, hoses
o: Bail with buckets until the water is out
Prepare the liferaft and grab bag on deck
Call MAYDAY at once, then look for the leak
why: Pump while you hunt: salt or fresh tells you a lot; check seacocks, hose clips, the stern gland and transducers.

fig.title: Water over the floorboards
lines: Water 10 cm over the cabin sole

q: The heads' inlet seacock has sheared off and water is spurting in. What do you do?
a: Hammer the bung tied to the fitting into the hole
o: Close the seacock handle as tight as it goes
Stuff a towel in the hole and hold it there
Tape over the hole from inside the hull
why: With the valve gone, only the tapered softwood bung will seal it — keep one tied beside every through-hull.

fig.title: Leak in the heads
lines: Softwood bung tied to the fitting

q: You are taking water through a damaged fitting you cannot reach. Can your pumps keep up with it?
a: Yes — both pumps together gain 17 L/min
o: No — each pump alone loses, so abandon
Yes — the electric pump alone gains 10 L/min
No — together they still lose 13 L/min
why: Manual: 0.6 × 45 = 27 L/min; with the electric 30 that is 57 L/min against 40 in — 17 L/min in hand.

fig.title: Leak below
lines: Manual pump: 0.6 L a stroke, 45 a min

q: It is 1630 and this is the state of things. What do you do now?
a: DSC alert and MAYDAY, raft ready, keep pumping aboard
o: Abandon to the raft at once while it is still light
Keep looking for the leak before making any call
Call PAN-PAN and ask for a pump to be dropped
why: Water you cannot stop is grave and imminent danger: call now, but stay with the yacht until you step up into the raft.

fig.title: Flooding
lines: 8 M off, wind F5, dark in 2 h

q: You must abandon ship and the raft is in its valise on deck. How do you launch and board it?
a: Painter fast, raft over to leeward, pull to inflate, step in dry
o: Raft over to windward first, then make the painter fast
Inflate it on the deck, then slide it over the rail
Painter fast, raft over, then jump into the sea to board
why: Tie the painter first or the raft is lost; launch to leeward, pull the painter to fire it, and step in from the deck.

fig.title: Abandon ship
lines: Raft in a valise on deck

q: You have sent the DSC distress alert and now make the voice call. After your identity, what comes next, in order?
a: Position, nature of distress, help needed, persons aboard
o: Nature of distress, persons aboard, position, help needed
Persons aboard, position, help needed, nature of distress
Help needed, position, persons aboard, nature of distress
why: Position first, so help can start even if the call breaks off; then what is wrong, what you need, how many aboard.

q: Your yacht is flooding fast and you need to send a distress alert now. What do you do?
a: Send the alert, then the MAYDAY with your position on 16
o: Reconnect the GPS first, then send the DSC alert
Send the MAYDAY with your position by voice on 70
Key in the position, then call MAYDAY on channel 13
why: Don't delay: the alert raises the alarm without a position; ch 70 is for DSC data only — voice and position go on 16.

q: On watch you see this. There is no traffic about it on channel 16. What do you do?
a: Note the bearing and time, then MAYDAY RELAY on 16
o: Note it in the log and carry on your course
Call the vessel that fired it on 16 and wait
Send a DSC distress alert with your own MMSI
why: You may be the only one who saw it: relay it with bearing and time; a DSC alert of your own would say you are in distress.

q: Your yacht has only a fixed VHF DSC set. Where can you count on a coast station receiving your DSC alert?
a: In area A1 — about 20–30 M from a VHF coast station
o: In area A2 — out to about 150 M from the coast
Anywhere, as the alert is relayed by satellite
Only within sight of the coast station's mast
why: VHF reaches a coast station only in sea area A1, typically 20–30 M; beyond it you rely on ships, MF or an EPIRB.

fig.title: GMDSS sea areas
lines: A1: in range of a VHF DSC coast station
A2: in range of an MF DSC coast station
Your passage: up to 40 M offshore

q: The rescue helicopter lowers its hi-line to your deck. What do you do with it?
a: Let it earth in the sea; hold it by hand, never tie it
o: Grab it at once and make it fast to a cleat
Take a turn round a winch to hold it steady
Tie it to the guardrail and stand well clear
why: Let it touch the water to discharge static; gather it in by hand — never make it fast, the aircraft may have to pull away.

fig.title: Helicopter rescue
lines: Winchman will come down on a hi-line
Weighted line lowered to the deck
Crew of 4 on deck, clipped on

q: A helicopter is coming to lift off your injured crew. How do you prepare the yacht?
a: Stow the bimini and loose gear; keep listening on 16
o: Light an orange smoke now and keep it burning
Drop all sail and lie beam-on to the wind
Fire a red rocket as it makes its approach
why: The downwash blows away anything loose; the pilot briefs you on 16 — course, speed and where the crew should be.

fig.title: Helicopter ETA 10 min
lines: Pilot will call you on VHF 16
Bimini up, dinghy on the foredeck

q: A lifeboat is about to pass you a towline. How do you make it fast?
a: To a bridle round strong points, led over the bow roller
o: To one bow cleat, with a turn for quick release
Round the forestay, held there by a crew member
To the stern cleats, so the bow stays free
why: Share the load over strong points with a bridle, lead it fair through the bow roller and protect it from chafe.

fig.title: Lifeboat tow
lines: Engine failure, 3 M off a lee shore
Bow cleats small; bow roller strong

q: You have 25 M to go, close-reaching under full sail with a furling genoa, and this forecast comes in. What do you do now?
a: Reef now and rig the storm jib while it is still easy
o: Wait for the gale, then reef everything at once
Roll the genoa to a scrap and leave it at that
Keep full sail to get in before the gale arrives
why: Reef and rig the storm jib early, in daylight and moderate wind; a deeply rolled genoa sets badly and can unroll.

q: You tack without releasing the jib to heave to and rest the crew. Where do you put the tiller and the main?
a: Tiller lashed to leeward, mainsheet eased
o: Tiller lashed to windward, main sheeted hard
Tiller amidships, main and jib both backed
Tiller lashed to leeward, main sheeted hard
why: The backed jib pushes the bow off and the rudder turns it up (tiller to leeward); ease the main so she lies quietly.

fig.note: Hove to: the jib backed after the tack

q: You are running off before a gale, surfing on the crests, with this sea room to leeward. How do you make it last?
a: Stream a drogue: the 21 M then last about 8 h 24 min
o: Keep running: 21 M last 3 h, and that will do
Stream a drogue: the 21 M then last about 4 h 40 min
Lie beam-on to the seas, so you use no sea room
why: 21 M ÷ 7 kn = 3 h, short of the 6 h; with a drogue 21 ÷ 2.5 = 8.4 h = 8 h 24 min, stern kept to the seas.

q: You are on a coastal passage with the coast to the east of you when this comes in. What do you do?
a: Head out to sea now, to gain sea room before the gale
o: Run for the harbour and cross its bar before dark
Anchor close under the coast and wait it out
Carry on along the coast as planned, 4 M off
why: A coast to leeward in a gale is the danger, and a bar breaks in an onshore blow — get sea room while you still can.

fig.title: Gale warning
lines: Only harbour: bar breaks in W 6 or more

q: One of your crew has been seasick since yesterday afternoon. What do you do?
a: Small sips of rehydration fluid, and get medical advice
o: Leave her in her bunk below until she recovers
Give her a big glass of water and a full meal
Put her on the helm to take her mind off it
why: Long vomiting dehydrates: small, frequent sips of rehydration salts, keep her warm, and get radio medical advice.

q: It is 2300 on passage in the Ionian and this is your situation. What is the safe decision?
a: Anchor in the sheltered bay, rest, and enter at daylight
o: Press on: the port has fuel, shops and showers
Press on, with the skipper on coffee at the helm
Heave to offshore until all the crew recover
why: Fatigue and seasickness cut judgement and hands; an unlit rocky entrance at night is the risk to avoid.

q: A fishing boat has just struck your port bow and backed off. What do you do first?
a: Check the crew for injuries, then the hull for damage
o: Get the other boat's name and details first
Chase the fishing boat to keep it in sight
Call MAYDAY at once, before anything else
why: People first, then the boat: a headcount and injuries, then look for water coming in — that decides which call to make.

fig.note: Just hit on the port bow

q: You have run onto a rock and this is what you find. What do you do?
a: Stem the leak and call for help before she floats
o: Motor astern at once to get her off the rock
Wait for high water to lift her, then inspect
Lay out the kedge and haul her off now
why: On the rock the leak is limited; afloat she may flood faster than you can pump. Stem it and call before she lifts.

fig.title: Aground on a rock
lines: Struck at 5 kn, 2 h before HW
Hole in the bow, water entering

q: Your engine dies halfway across the north-east-going lane of a traffic separation scheme, as the chart shows. What do you do?
a: Call PAN-PAN and tell the VTS and the ship where you are
o: Anchor in the lane until the engine is fixed
Work on the engine and call only if the ship is close
Call MAYDAY and launch the raft as a precaution
why: Unable to keep clear in a shipping lane is urgency, not distress: a PAN-PAN tells ships and the VTS so they can act.

q: Your engine stops off a rocky lee shore with the sails still in their covers. How long have you got, and what do you do first?
a: About 20 min: anchor now, then call PAN-PAN
o: About 33 min: call PAN-PAN, then try the engine
About 3 min: abandon to the raft at once
About 20 min: work on the engine, then decide
why: 4 cables = 0.4 M; 0.4 ÷ 1.2 kn = 0.33 h = 20 min. In 12 m with 50 m of chain, anchor first to stop the drift.

q: You have pulled a swimmer out after several minutes under water. What do you do?
a: Open the airway, give five rescue breaths, then CPR
o: Chest compressions only, with no breaths at all
Roll him on his front to drain out the water
Recovery position, then wait for help to come
why: A drowned casualty is short of oxygen: five rescue breaths first, then 30 compressions to 2 breaths — and the MAYDAY.

q: A crew member has been hit on the head by the boom in a gybe. What do you do?
a: Call PAN-PAN for medical advice and watch him closely
o: Let him sleep it off alone in his bunk
Give him painkillers and carry on the passage
Wait until you are in port to have him seen
why: Knocked out, then confused and vomiting: signs of a serious head injury — urgency call for radio medical advice.

fig.title: Hit by the boom
lines: Knocked out for about a minute

q: A crew member falls into the cockpit and hurts her forearm. You open the first-aid kit. What do you do?
a: Splint it as you find it, sling it, check her fingers
o: Pull the arm straight first, then splint it
Leave it free so that she can still work
Rub it well, then bandage it on tightly
why: Support the limb as you find it — never straighten it; splint and sling, then check circulation beyond the injury.

q: A pot of boiling water slides off the stove onto a crew member's forearm. What do you do?
a: Cool it under cool clean water for 20 minutes
o: Cover it with butter or a greasy cream
Burst the blisters, then dry the skin
Hold ice on it for about a minute
why: Cool with clean cool water for 20 min, then cover loosely with cling film; no creams, no ice, leave blisters intact.

q: Your mast has just been struck by lightning and the crew are all unhurt. What do you check next?
a: The hull and through-hulls for leaks
o: The VHF and plotter for damage
The masthead lights and wind gear
The compass deviation on each heading
why: A strike can blow out a through-hull or the hull near the keel; check the bilge first — electronics and compass after.

q: You pass this in the approach to a busy harbour. What call do you make?
a: SÉCURITÉ, to warn other vessels
o: MAYDAY, as it is a danger to all
PAN-PAN, as your own boat is at risk
No call — a note in the log will do
why: A hazard to navigation is a safety message: SÉCURITÉ, giving what it is and where.

fig.title: Hazard sighted
lines: 3 M south of the harbour entrance

q: A crew member has slipped off the stern at anchor in a calm bay, water 24°C. She is fit and swimming to the stern swim ladder. The engine is ticking over in neutral. What do you do?
a: Stop the engine before she reaches the ladder
o: Leave it in neutral, ready to manoeuvre
Go slow astern to close the gap to her
Go slow ahead so the boat holds her head
why: The propeller turns a few feet under the swim ladder; neutral can be knocked into gear — engine off before a swimmer comes near.

fig.title: Calm anchorage, 1100
lines: Crew fell off the stern 2 min ago
Water 24°C, she is fit and swimming

q: You skipper a 12 m catamaran and motor back to a man overboard on both engines. Where do you bring him to get him aboard?
a: To the stern steps of one hull, that engine stopped
o: Between the hulls, under the bridgedeck
To the bows, in the gap between the hulls
Amidships, over the side-deck guardrail
why: The low transom steps are the easiest way up; between the hulls the bridgedeck can slam down on him — and stop the prop by him.

q: In the debrief of tonight's MOB drill you read this. What do you change for the next one?
a: The pointer only points, and does nothing else
o: The pointer also helps to roll the genoa away
The helm takes over pointing as well as steering
Nobody points; the plotter's MOB mark is enough
why: A small light at night is lost in seconds: one crew keeps eyes and arm on the casualty and is given no other job.

fig.title: Drill debrief, 2240
lines: Fender with a light thrown at 2210
Pointer helped to roll the genoa

q: In the drill debrief you look at the times. How far along your track from where the fender went in did the MOB waypoint go?
a: About 0.3 M: press MOB the moment he goes
o: About 1.8 M: press MOB the moment he goes
About 0.18 M: press MOB the moment he goes
None: the plotter marks the moment he fell
why: Three minutes at 6.0 kn: 6.0 × 3/60 = 0.3 M — the waypoint marks where you pressed, not where he fell.

q: Under sail a crew has gone over and you are about to start the engine to go back. What do you check first?
a: That no sheets or lines are trailing in the water
o: That the engine's oil level is up to the mark
That the fuel tank has enough for an hour
That the plotter's MOB mark is on the screen
why: A rope round the propeller leaves you without an engine just when you need it — look over the side before you engage gear.

fig.title: MOB under sail
lines: Genoa sheet washed over the side

q: You are running under spinnaker in F4 when a crew member goes over the side. After shouting and the danbuoy, what is your plan?
a: Press MOB, get the spinnaker down, then turn back
o: Gybe at once with the spinnaker set, and head back
Round up hard with the spinnaker still drawing
Keep running until the spinnaker is packed below
why: You cannot come back upwind under a spinnaker; drop it at once (a pointer on him all the time), then return under main or engine.

fig.note: Running under spinnaker, F4 — a crew has gone over

q: Your man overboard is alongside on a line, exhausted and too heavy to lift by hand. You have no lifting strop. How do you get him aboard level?
a: Roll him up in a sail on a halyard: a parbuckle
o: Two crew haul him up the topsides by his arms
A bowline round his chest, winched up upright
Wait until he recovers and climbs the ladder
why: A sail with its foot made fast on deck and a halyard on the other edge rolls him up horizontally — no vertical lift after immersion.

fig.title: Casualty alongside
lines: 20 min in water at 14°C, very tired
Too heavy to lift by hand

q: At night you find your danbuoy with its light, but there is no sign of the man it was thrown to. Where do you search first?
a: At A, upwind of the danbuoy
o: At B, downwind of the danbuoy
At C, across the wind to the north
At D, across the wind to the south
why: Both drift with the stream, but the tall danbuoy blows downwind faster than a swimmer: he is likely to windward of it.

fig.note: Night · thrown beside him 20 min ago · wind W F5

q: Tidying the chart table, a crew member presses the DSC distress button and the alert goes out. Nothing is wrong. What do you do?
a: Cancel it on the set, then tell all stations on 16
o: Switch the set off and make no further call
Send a second alert marked 'test' on channel 70
Wait for the MRCC to call you, then explain
why: Stop the alert, then a voice call on 16: ALL STATIONS, your name, call sign and MMSI, cancel my distress alert of (time UTC).

fig.title: False alert
lines: DSC distress alert sent by mistake

q: You are about to call the marina on channel 16 when you hear this. What do you do?
a: Keep off 16 unless you can help with the distress
o: Make the marina call — a short one is allowed
Reply 'SEELONCE MAYDAY' to show you heard
Switch off the VHF until the coastguard is done
why: SEELONCE MAYDAY imposes silence on the channel for the distress; keep listening in case you can help.

fig.title: Channel 16, 1120
lines: A MAYDAY is being worked by the MRCC

q: An hour later, after the distress you heard, the MRCC sends this on 16. What does it mean?
a: The distress is over; 16 is back to normal use
o: Restricted working: urgent calls only on 16
The casualty is still missing; keep silent
Silence on 16 for one more hour from now
why: SEELONCE FEENEE ends distress traffic; PRUDONCE would mean restricted working may resume while the distress continues.

q: Your DSC set sounds this alarm. No coast station has answered on 16 after a few minutes. What do you do?
a: Listen on 16; with no coast station, acknowledge by voice
o: Acknowledge at once by DSC from your own set
Relay it at once by DSC to all ships
Leave it — the coast station will deal with it
why: A yacht does not acknowledge a distress alert by DSC: listen on 16, and if no coast station answers, acknowledge by voice and tell the MRCC.

q: You plan this crossing with a fixed VHF DSC set and a 406 MHz EPIRB. How much of it lies outside sea area A1, and what alerts the MRCC there?
a: The middle 20 M; the EPIRB still raises the MRCC
o: The middle 45 M; the EPIRB still raises the MRCC
None of it; A1 covers 60 M off any coast
The middle 20 M; nothing can raise the MRCC there
why: 70 − 2 × 25 = 20 M out of reach of a coast station by VHF; the EPIRB works by satellite anywhere, and ships nearby still hear your DSC.

fig.title: Crossing plan
lines: Each coast: VHF DSC station, A1 ≈ 25 M

q: You are dismasted and rig your spare VHF aerial. Can you still reach the coast station?
a: No — about 24 M now: call ships nearby
o: Yes — still about 29 M, as from the masthead
No — about 4 M now: only for ships alongside
Yes — about 40 M now, with plenty in hand
why: 2.2 × (√4 + √81) = 2.2 × 11 = 24.2 M, short of 26 M; from the 16 m masthead it was 2.2 × 13 = 28.6 M.

fig.title: Dismasted
lines: Spare aerial on the pushpit: 4 m

q: Your GPS has failed and you fix by this light. In the MAYDAY you give your position from it. What do you say?
a: 220°T from the light, 4.0 M
o: 040°T from the light, 4.0 M
226°T from the light, 4.0 M
223°T from the light, 4.0 M
why: 043°M − 3°W = 040°T to the light, so you lie on the reciprocal from it: 040 + 180 = 220°T, 4.0 M.

q: Ten minutes ago you sent a PAN-PAN. Now this is your situation. What do you do?
a: MAYDAY now: about 30 min to the rocks
o: Keep the PAN-PAN: about 50 min to the rocks
Keep the PAN-PAN: about 2 h to the rocks
MAYDAY now: about 5 min to the rocks
why: 0.3 M ÷ 0.6 kn = 0.5 h = 30 min; a crewed yacht about to go on rocks at night is grave and imminent danger.

q: You are searching for a liferaft and your radar shows this. Where is the raft?
a: Near the dot nearest to you, on 300°
o: At the far end of the line of dots
In the middle of the line of dots
At the dot just beyond the nearest
why: A SART answers your radar with 12 dots running outward; the one nearest to you marks it. Close in, the dots become arcs, then rings.

fig.title: Radar, 12 M range
lines: No other echo on that bearing

q: Your crew has been in the water for a few minutes and has switched on his PLB. How should he hold it?
a: Out of the water, aerial up, held as high as he can
o: Inside his lifejacket, where it stays dry
Floating beside him on its lanyard
Flat on his chest under the lifejacket
why: A PLB's 406 MHz and GNSS antennas need open sky: aerial vertical, clear of the water and of his body.

q: Your yacht has the AIS fitted as on this card. Crossing a shipping lane at night, can the ships see you on their AIS?
a: No — a receiver sends nothing; only a transponder is seen
o: Yes — any AIS set shows on the ships' screens
Yes — but only within about 2 M of the ship
Only if the VHF is switched to channel 16
why: A receive-only AIS shows you the ships; to appear on theirs you need a Class B (or A) transponder.

q: At night a red parachute rocket is needed and the cloud is low. How do you fire it?
a: At about 45°, downwind, so it burns under the cloud
o: Straight up, as for a clear night sky
Into the wind, so it drifts back over you
Two at once, straight up, to be sure
why: A rocket climbs about 300 m; in low cloud angle it 45° downwind (it turns into the wind) so the flare hangs below the cloud base.

q: You are becalmed with no engine at night. This ship is closing and does not answer on 16. Which flare do you use?
a: A white handheld flare, to show you are there
o: A red parachute rocket, to make her stop
An orange smoke, as her radar can see it
A red handheld flare, held over the bow
why: A white flare warns of collision; red flares mean distress and would start a rescue you do not need.

fig.note: 0230 · bearing steady, about 1 M · no engine, no wind

q: At the pre-season check one crew's lifejacket shows this. What do you do?
a: Re-arm it with a new cylinder and cap before use
o: Nothing — a red indicator shows it is armed
Tighten the cylinder by hand and wear it
Blow it up by mouth before each watch instead
why: Red (or a missing clip) means fired or not armed; fit a new rearming kit and screw the cylinder home.

fig.title: Lifejacket check
lines: Gas cylinder: loose in its thread

q: Your liferaft sits in a deck cradle like this. If the yacht sinks before anyone can launch it, what happens?
a: The release frees it, it floats up and inflates
o: Nothing — it can only be launched by hand
It inflates in its cradle and stays there
It goes down with her, held by the painter
why: At a few metres' depth the hydrostatic release lets go; the painter pulls to fire the gas, then the weak link breaks.

fig.title: Liferaft stowage
lines: Painter tied to the HRU weak link

q: All four of you are in the raft beside your sinking yacht. What do you do now?
a: Cut the painter, get clear, stream the drogue
o: Stay tied on to her until she goes under
Get clear, close up, and drift with no drogue
Cut free and paddle hard for the coast
why: A sinking hull can pull the raft down or hole it; once clear, the drogue steadies the raft and keeps it near the alert position.

fig.title: In the raft
lines: Yacht low in the water, sinking
Wind W F5, coast 20 M east

q: Your liferaft has inflated upside down beside you in the water. How do you right it?
a: Climb onto the gas bottle side and pull the righting strap
o: Swim under it and push the floor up from below
Board it as it is and wait for it to flip
Cut a hole in the floor to let the air out
why: Stand on the cylinder, hold the righting strap and lean back; the raft comes over towards you — then swim clear from under it.

fig.title: Raft capsized
lines: Crew in the water, lifejackets on

q: You will step into the raft in two minutes. The grab bag is packed as listed. What else do you take?
a: Extra water, warm clothes and the EPIRB
o: The ship's papers, passports and cash
The plotter, unscrewed from the chart table
Tins of food from the galley lockers
why: Water and warmth keep you alive; the EPIRB brings the rescue. Papers can be replaced; food matters far less than water.

fig.title: Grab bag
lines: EPIRB still in its bracket below

q: Your crew want to take to the liferaft. This is the state of things. What do you decide?
a: Stay aboard — the yacht is a far safer raft
o: Take to the raft now, while it is light
Put two crew in the raft, tied on astern
Take to the raft once the MRCC agrees
why: Step up into the raft only when the yacht is sinking or on fire; a sound, dry hull is bigger, warmer and easier to find.

q: A cushion in the saloon is smouldering where a candle fell on it. Which extinguisher do you use?
a: Foam or water — they cool it so it will not flare again
o: CO2 — it leaves no mess on the upholstery
Dry powder, then leave it to cool by itself
None — throw it into the cockpit as it is
why: A class A fire (solids) is put out by cooling: water or foam; powder and CO2 knock it down but it can reignite.

fig.title: Smouldering cushion
lines: Candle fell on a saloon cushion
Aboard: dry powder, CO2, foam, bucket

q: You are fitting out a yacht for a season of coastal passages. Where do you mount the fire extinguishers?
a: By each exit, so the way out is behind you
o: All together in the engine bay, by the risk
In a cockpit locker, away from the heat
Over the stove, where most fires start
why: Fight a fire with your escape behind you: one by the companionway, one by the forehatch, the blanket by the galley.

fig.title: Fitting out
lines: Galley aft, engine under the steps

q: You are fitting a gas alarm in a yacht with an LPG cooker. Where do you put its sensor?
a: Low down near the cooker, just above the bilge
o: High up over the cooker, at the deckhead
In the gas locker on deck, by the bottle
At head height by the companionway steps
why: LPG is heavier than air and collects low, so the sensor goes below the cooker, under floor level, clear of bilge water.

fig.title: Gas alarm
lines: Bottle in a deck locker, drained overboard

q: You have fitted a new gas regulator and want to check the joints for leaks. How?
a: Soapy water on each joint, with the bottle on
o: A lit match held close to each joint
Sniff each joint with the bottle turned off
Light the cooker and watch the flame colour
why: Bubbles show a leak; never use a flame. Many systems also carry a bubble tester or gauge to check the whole line.

fig.title: New regulator
lines: Hose and joints to the cooker

q: It is a cold, wet evening at anchor and these are the symptoms below. What do you suspect and do?
a: Carbon monoxide — everyone into fresh air now
o: Seasickness — give them tablets and rest
Dehydration — water and an early night
Gas leak — run the hand bilge pump
why: Headache, drowsiness and nausea in a closed cabin with an engine or heater running point to CO; ventilate, get out, stop the source.

q: The bilge alarm goes off and you find this. Where do you look first?
a: The fresh-water tanks, pipes and pump
o: Every seacock, closing them one by one
The stern gland, tightening it at once
The deck fittings and mast step for rain
why: Fresh water and a pump that runs by itself point to the domestic system: switch the pump off and look for the leaking pipe.

fig.title: Water in the bilge
lines: Bilge water tastes fresh, not salt
Pressure pump runs on its own

q: Your two bilge pumps are losing to the leak. You close the engine's raw-water seacock and put its intake hose in the bilge, engine running. Where do you stand now?
a: Gaining about 27 L/min
o: Losing about 13 L/min
Level: 70 in and 70 out
Gaining about 97 L/min
why: Out: 30 + 27 + 40 = 97 L/min against 70 in — 27 L/min in hand. Keep a strainer on the hose so debris does not stop the engine.

q: A collision has holed your port bow just above the waterline, and water comes in on every wave. You must sail 12 M to port. How do you sail?
a: On port tack, so she heels to starboard
o: On starboard tack, so she heels to port
Under engine, upright, at full speed
Dead downwind, so she sits upright
why: Heel her so the damaged side lifts: wind on the port side heels her to starboard and lifts the port bow clear.

fig.title: Holed
lines: Hole in the port bow, just above the WL
Wind W F4; port 12 M to the north

q: You touch a sandbank and stop, with the tide falling. What do you do at once?
a: Go astern now, crew on the boom to heel her
o: Wait — she will float off on the next tide
Call MAYDAY first, then try to get off
Lay out the kedge, then wait a few hours
why: On a falling tide every minute makes it worse: try at once, astern along your track, heeled to cut the draught.

fig.title: Aground on sand
lines: Draught 1.9 m, depth at the bow 1.8 m

q: She would not come off and will dry out on this bank before the next flood. How do you let her lie?
a: Heeled to the shallow side, padded, kedge out to deep water
o: Heeled to the deep side, so she slides off later
Upright, and let her fall whichever way she goes
Heeled to the deep side, kedge laid towards the shallows
why: Lying up the slope, her low side sits higher, so the flood lifts her before it reaches the coamings; the kedge stops her driving further on.

fig.note: Bank slopes down to the east

q: The gale is at its height and the crew suggest this to get some rest. What do you say?
a: No — beam-on, a breaking crest can roll her
o: Yes — with no sail up she cannot be knocked down
Yes — the keel keeps her stable beam-on
Yes — once all the crew are below, hatch shut
why: Lying a-hull leaves her beam-on to the seas; in breaking seas that is how yachts are rolled. Heave to or run off instead.

fig.title: Gale, 0400
lines: W gale 8–9, seas 5 m, crests breaking
Suggestion: drop all sail, lie a-hull

q: You have to ride out this gale. Which tactic fits the sea room you have?
a: Heave to: about 15 M of the 30 M used
o: Run off: 30 M ÷ 5 kn = 6 h, so that fits
Heave to: only about 1.5 M of drift in all
Lie a-hull: she uses no sea room at all
why: Running: 10 h × 5 kn = 50 M, more than the 30 M; hove to: 10 h × 1.5 kn = 15 M, well inside it.

fig.title: Gale tactics
lines: Sea room to the SW: 30 M
Bare poles: 5 kn; hove to: 1.5 kn drift

q: A seasick crew member needs to be sick over the side during her night watch. Where and how?
a: Clipped on in the cockpit, a bucket, someone by her
o: Unclipped at the lee rail, so she can lean out
Alone on the foredeck, away from the others
Down in the forepeak bunk with a bowl
why: Seasick crew are weak and slow — a classic MOB at night; keep her clipped on, in the cockpit, and watched.

fig.title: Night watch, 0130
lines: Lee rail low in the water

q: A crew member who is often seasick joins you for tomorrow's 0600 start. When should he take his seasickness tablet?
a: Some hours before sailing, as the packet says
o: Once he first feels queasy at sea
Only after he has been sick once
Only if the forecast is F5 or more
why: Tablets work to prevent seasickness, not to cure it — once vomiting starts they are not kept down.

q: Your engine dies off this lee shore, but the sails are ready to hoist. How long have you got, and what do you do?
a: About 40 min: set sail and claw off, then report
o: About 67 min: work on the engine before sailing
About 90 min: wait and see if she drifts clear
About 40 min: call MAYDAY and wait for help
why: 1.0 M ÷ 1.5 kn = 0.67 h = 40 min — time enough to hoist sail and beat off; tell the coastguard once you are clear.

q: You take over a yacht the day before a night passage. When do you find out how her emergency tiller fits?
a: Now, by fitting it once alongside the pontoon
o: When the steering fails, from the manual
Never — the base fits it if it is needed
Only if the wheel starts to feel stiff
why: In the dark with the boat rolling is no time to learn; fit it once in harbour and know where it lives.

q: Your catamaran has capsized in a squall and floats upside down. The crew are all accounted for. What do you do?
a: Stay with the hull — get in through the escape hatch
o: Swim for the shore, 3 M away, together
Launch the raft and leave her at once
Dive inside to fetch the VHF from the saloon
why: An unballasted catamaran floats when inverted: stay with it, shelter in the hull via the escape hatch, set off the EPIRB.

fig.title: Capsized catamaran
lines: Inverted after a squall, floating high
Crew of 4 in the water by the hulls
Coast 3 M; EPIRB in the grab bag

q: This crew member is getting worse and you will call for radio medical advice. What do you have written down before you call?
a: Pulse, breathing, temperature, history, kit list
o: Only your position — the doctor asks the rest
Her passport, insurance and next of kin
The marina's phone number and your ETA there
why: The doctor can only advise on what you report: the signs, what happened, medicines given, what is in your kit — and your position.

q: You pulled this crew member out after a minute under water. Now he says he feels fine. What do you do?
a: Get medical advice — trouble can follow hours later
o: Nothing more — he is breathing and talking
Let him sleep it off alone in his bunk
A hot drink and back to his watch
why: Water in the lungs can cause breathing problems hours afterwards: anyone who has inhaled water needs a doctor's view.

q: You have recovered this man overboard. How do you handle him?
a: Keep him flat, move him gently, insulate him
o: Sit him up and give him a hot sweet drink
Put him in a hot shower to rewarm him fast
Rub his arms and legs to get the blood moving
why: Severe hypothermia: rough handling or sitting up can stop the heart; no drinks when unconscious. Lie him flat, wrap him, get help.

q: You have cooled this scald under water for 20 minutes. What next?
a: Cover it loosely with cling film; get medical advice
o: Burst the blisters and leave it open to the air
A fluffy dressing taped down firmly over it
Burn cream on it, and carry on the passage
why: A burn larger than the casualty's palm, or on the hand, needs a doctor: cling film laid on, not wrapped tight.

fig.title: Galley scald
lines: Boiling water over forearm and hand

q: The helicopter pilot tells you your mast and rigging make a deck lift unsafe. What may he ask you to do?
a: Put the casualty in the dinghy on a long line astern
o: Cut the backstay so the winchman can land
Lower the mast before he makes his approach
Lie beam-on and stop the engine for the lift
why: On a yacht the rig can foul the winch wire; the lift is often made from the dinghy or raft streamed well astern.

fig.title: Helicopter on scene
lines: Pilot: mast too close for a deck lift

q: A thunderstorm is coming towards you and you cannot avoid it. How do you prepare?
a: Crew below, clear of the mast; spare handhelds in the oven
o: All on deck, holding the shrouds to earth themselves
Hoist full sail to outrun it for the harbour
Go up the mast and unplug the VHF aerial
why: Keep people off the rig and its chainplates; disconnect what you can, and keep a handheld VHF and GPS in the oven as a shielded spare.
